newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND-US manufacturing growth seen slowing in 97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-US manufacturing growth seen slowing in 97.

text.p: A modest increase in demand for factory items should limit expansion of U.S. manufacturing in 1997 -- and possibly for the next couple of years -- according to the projections of several economists.
"It won't be a strong year for manufacturing, but it won't be as weak as 1995 or the past couple of months," said Donald Maude, chief U.S. economist at Scotia Capital Markets Inc.

Manufacturers expect a 5.4 percent nominal gain in revenue growth next year, according to a survey released this week by the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM). That compares with a reported 4.9 percent revenue increase in 1996 and 7.4 percent in 1994, NAPM said.

Economists said they expect factory output growth to be Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp, echoed other economists in forecasting a 2.0 to 2.5 percent expansion in industrial production next year on a fourth-quarter over fourth-quarter basis. Industry output grew by about 3.75 percent in 1996, Hoffman said.
Economic data in recent months suggests output growth has slowed in the current quarter compared with the third, largely because of overgrown inventories, analysts said.
Manufacturing output fell 0.5 percent in October, the latest reported month, while business inventories grew 0.5 percent, their largest increase since January.

However, signs of a near-term rebound are emerging. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta's November index of industry business activity, for example, showed a pickup in new orders and a decline in inventories.
Probably the greatest factor in determining the pace of manufacturing next year will be demand, which economists said should grow only slightly from 1996 levels.
"The demand situation out there is growth, but not runaway growth," Ralph Kauffman, chairman of NAPM's business survey committee, told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday.
Automobile manufacturing, reflecting tepid demand, might actually contract in 1997 after a good performance this year, some economists said.

"In my outlook for next year, I have consumers making fewer purchases of cars and trucks than they did this year," said PNC's Hoffman, who called for a decline of about 4.0 to 5.0 percent in car and light truck purchases.
"If it goes into a car or has anything to do with a car, my guess is, that sector of manufacturing will be flat to down next year," Hoffman added.

Housing probably will decline next year as well, the PNC economist said. Those two industries account for about 10 percent of manufacturing, so declines in them would weigh heavily on the factory sector as a whole.

Capital expenditures are expected to decrease next year, according to NAPM's outlook survey. Purchasing executives, on average, said they would spend 1.6 percent less on capital items in 1997, compared with a 13.5 percent increase reported for 1996.
Economists said the planned capital spending cut fits into a typical ebb-and-flow cycle and may hint at a slower growth trend for at least the next couple of years.
"When you have companies have an increase one year, they tend to see a smaller increase the following year," said NAPM's Kauffman, who is a professor of purchasing at the University of Houston.

Manufacturing can still grow if capital spending is cut, economists said. A cutback simply indicates factory owners do not expect output growth substantial enough to push against their maximum production capacity ceiling.

Purchasers surveyed by NAPM reported running at 86.8 percent of capacity as of December 1996, which leaves room for some output growth in 1997. "Back in 1994, when things were really booming, we had capacity utilized reported at 89.5 percent," Kauffman said.
But a drop in projected capital outlay does suggest manufacturers expect the growth rate of demand to continue to shrink, PNC's Hoffman said.
"I think it means they're looking for slower growth over the next couple of years, not just 1997," he said.
--N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660
